passage: I sit two desks from Pankaj, so I saw the whole thing on Thursday. Uma was building the vendor comparison sheet, and it was slow going: she kept stopping and rereading. Pankaj's chair squeaked more than usual. Twice he leaned toward her mouse, then pulled back and picked up his pen. Around four he said, "Show me where you're stuck," and just listened while she explained her formula. Then, "What would you try first?" She tried it, and it worked. Uma grinned. Pankaj smiled too, though his knuckles still looked tight. As I passed his desk he said, half laughing, "If I'd grabbed it, she still wouldn't know the formula." I can't say what he felt. But the sheet went out under Uma's name.

qa.q: What was Uma building on Thursday?
qa.a: Uma was building the vendor comparison sheet.

qa.q: What might Pankaj have been feeling when he leaned toward Uma's mouse, and what cue points to it?
qa.a: He may have been impatient and tempted to take the task back, since he reached twice and pulled back. The narrator admits they cannot be sure. 🤔

qa.q: Why did asking "What would you try first?" work better than taking over the sheet?
qa.a: It let Uma reason it out and learn the formula, so the result was hers. Taking over would have left her not knowing it.

qa.q: How might Uma have felt if Pankaj had taken over her mouse?
qa.a: She might have felt small or distrusted, and she would have lost the chance to learn.

grounding: Shows a colleague watching a senior fight the urge to take a task back from a junior and coach instead.

passage:
Monday. Jahnavi's first draft of the market report landed in Nilesh's inbox two hours late, and the charts were wrong. Nilesh felt his jaw tighten. It would take him forty minutes to redo it himself. He almost did. Instead he wrote three comments and sent it back.

Thursday. The second draft was better but still messy. "Just give it to me, I'll finish it," Nilesh heard himself say out loud. Jahnavi's face fell. He caught himself. "Actually, no. Sit with me for twenty minutes. Show me how you built chart three." She explained; he asked questions; she fixed it herself.

Three weeks later. Jahnavi sent the monthly report on time, with a note: "I added a new comparison chart. Is it useful?" It was. Nilesh forwarded it to his manager with her name on it.

He still felt the itch to take things back sometimes. He just didn't scratch it.

qa.q: How late was Jahnavi's first draft?
qa.a: Jahnavi's first draft was two hours late.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling when his jaw tightened on Monday?
qa.a: Nilesh felt irritated and impatient, tempted to redo the report himself because it would be faster.

qa.q: What changed on Thursday, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Nilesh stopped himself from taking the task back and coached Jahnavi instead, so she learned to fix it herself.

qa.q: What was it like for Jahnavi when Nilesh said "Just give it to me"?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt deflated and discouraged; her face fell, as if her effort didn't count.

grounding: Shows a senior irritated by a junior's work, tempted to take the task back, learning that doing it for them stunts growth.

passage:
Rukmini, you're asking why I don't just fix your slides myself. Let your old Shankar sir tell you why.

When I was twenty-five, I had my first junior at the bank, a boy called Farooq. He was slow. Every loan file he prepared, I would sigh, take it home and redo it at night. I thought I was being helpful, and also, honestly, I was irritated.

After six months my manager asked Farooq to prepare a file alone while I was on leave. He couldn't. He sat at his desk for two days, afraid to ask anyone. When I came back he said, "Sir, you never let me finish anything."

That hit me hard. I had taken away every chance he had to learn.

From that day I gave the files back with notes, not corrections. It was slower for three months. Then Farooq became the best file-maker in the branch.

So, your slides go back to you. With notes.

qa.q: Where did young Shankar work when Farooq was his junior?
qa.a: Young Shankar worked at the bank.

qa.q: What was young Shankar feeling when he took Farooq's files home to redo?
qa.a: Young Shankar felt irritated with Farooq's slowness, while also believing he was being helpful.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what did young Shankar choose to do after it?
qa.a: Farooq couldn't prepare a file alone and said he was never allowed to finish anything; Shankar then returned files with notes instead of redoing them.

qa.q: How did Farooq feel when he had to prepare a file alone?
qa.a: Farooq felt afraid and stuck, sitting at his desk for two days without daring to ask for help.

grounding: Shows through an elder's memory how taking a junior's work back out of irritation stunts growth, and how giving it back with notes helps.
